answer: A traditional Finnish or Estonian sauna is usually heated to 70–90 °C at bench level. Beginners feel most comfortable around 60–70 °C. Remember that the upper bench is noticeably hotter than the lower one, so you can control the heat simply by changing where you sit.

Löyly – called leil in Estonian – is the burst of steam you get by ladling water onto the hot stones. Start with half a ladle, wait for the wave of heat to reach you, then add more if everyone agrees. Always ask the others before throwing – it is good sauna manners.

For your first visit: shower first, take a towel to sit on, and start on the lower bench. Stay 5–10 minutes, then cool down outside or in a cool shower, rest and drink water. Two or three rounds is plenty. Listen to your body and leave whenever you feel uncomfortable.

topic: How long and how many rounds
answer: A typical round in the hot room lasts 8–15 minutes, followed by a cool-down and a rest about as long as the heating round. Most people do 2–4 rounds. There is no need to compete – shorter rounds are perfectly fine.
You lose a lot of fluid through sweat, often 0.5–1 litre per session. Drink a glass of water before you start and between rounds. Water, herbal tea or a mild mineral drink are good choices.

Avoid alcohol before and during sauna. Alcohol together with heat lowers blood pressure, dehydrates you and increases the risk of fainting, falls and heart rhythm problems. Enjoy a cold drink of water instead – and save the beer for much later, if at all.

Cooling down is half of the sauna ritual. Options: a cool shower, a swim in a lake or the sea, rolling in snow or an ice hole (avanto). If you are new to cold plunges, start gently with a cool shower and keep cold dips short. People with heart conditions should ask a doctor before cold plunges.

A vihta (Estonian: viht) is a bundle of fresh birch branches. Gently patting the skin with a warmed whisk improves circulation and releases a fresh birch scent. Soak it in warm water for a few minutes before use; dried whisks need a longer soak in hot water.

Fresh whisks are made in early summer when birch leaves are soft and strong. To store them, either dry them in a cool, airy and shady place, or wrap them in a bag and freeze them. A frozen whisk is thawed in warm water and feels almost like a fresh one.

A smoke sauna has no chimney: the stove heats a large pile of stones for several hours while the smoke fills the room, then the smoke is let out before bathing. The heat is soft and long-lasting. The Võro smoke sauna tradition in South Estonia is on UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The main sauna heaters are wood-burning stoves (classic feel, softer steam, need a chimney), electric heaters (easy and clean, controlled by a thermostat) and continuous-heat vs. heat-storing models. For a home sauna, pick the heater power according to the room volume – roughly 1 kW per 1–1.5 m³ for a well-insulated room.

Use rocks made for sauna heaters, such as peridotite, olivine diabase or vulcanite. Check the stones once a year and replace cracked or crumbling ones – broken stones block air flow and can damage an electric heater. Rinse new stones before stacking them loosely, with air gaps between them.

Benches are usually made from aspen, alder or heat-treated wood because they stay cooler to the touch and have few knots or resin. Walls are often spruce or pine panelling. Avoid varnish on benches – use only sauna oil or wax made for sauna surfaces.

Good ventilation keeps the air fresh and the löyly pleasant. A common setup has a fresh-air inlet low near the heater and an exhaust vent high on the opposite wall or low under the bench. Ventilate and dry the sauna after every use to prevent mould.

After each use leave the door and vents open so the room dries. Every few weeks wash benches with mild soap or a special sauna cleaner and a soft brush. Always sit on a towel – it keeps the benches clean. Sand off dark stains lightly once a year.

topic: How long does it take to heat
keywords: heat up;heating;preheat;warm up;how long to heat;ready
answer: An electric sauna usually heats up in 30–60 minutes. A wood-burning sauna takes about 45–90 minutes, depending on the stove, the wood and the outdoor temperature. A smoke sauna needs 4–6 hours of heating.

Shower before entering, sit on a towel, ask before throwing more löyly and keep your voice low. In Finnish and Estonian public saunas men and women usually have separate rooms and people bathe nude; in mixed saunas swimsuits or towels are common. Follow the local rules.

Regular sauna bathing helps many people relax, sleep better and recover after exercise. Some long-term studies link frequent sauna use to better cardiovascular health. It is not a medical treatment, though – think of it as part of a healthy lifestyle.

Most people with stable, well-treated blood pressure can enjoy sauna, but heat lowers blood pressure and raises the heart rate. If you have a heart condition, recent heart attack, chest pain or take blood-pressure medication, ask your doctor first, keep rounds short and avoid sudden cold plunges.

Many people continue mild sauna bathing during a normal pregnancy, but recommendations vary. Ask your doctor or midwife first, use a lower temperature, keep rounds short and leave immediately if you feel dizzy or unwell.

Children can go to the sauna with an adult, on the lower bench and at a lower temperature, for only a few minutes at a time. Always supervise them, give them water to drink and never leave a child alone in the sauna.

If you feel dizzy, sick or get a headache, leave the sauna at once, sit or lie down somewhere cool, drink water and rest. Do not go back in that day. Get medical help if the symptoms are severe or do not pass.

You can add a few drops of a sauna aroma made for sauna use to the löyly water – birch, tar, eucalyptus and pine are classics. Never pour pure essential oil on the stones; it can ignite or irritate your airways. Always dilute it in water first.

Keep towels, clothes and wood away from the heater. Check the safety distances given by the stove manufacturer, sweep the chimney regularly and install a smoke detector in the dressing room. Never dry clothes above the stove.

If an electric heater stops heating, check the fuse and the timer first. Old, crumbling stones can overheat the elements, so re-stack the stones regularly. Any electrical repairs must be done by a qualified electrician.

In Estonia the sauna has long been a place to wash, rest, heal and even give birth. Families heat the sauna on Saturdays and especially on Midsummer's Eve (jaanipäev). Common Estonian words: saun (sauna), leil (steam), viht (whisk) and kerise (stove).

Finland has millions of saunas for about 5.6 million people. Finnish sauna culture is listed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. For Finns the sauna is a place of peace – an old saying holds that in the sauna you should behave as you would in church.

After your last round, rest until you stop sweating before you dress. Drink water and enjoy a light snack – salty food helps restore lost minerals. Many people find they sleep especially well after an evening sauna.

For a home sauna, plan for at least 1 m² of bench space per bather. Use proper insulation and a vapour barrier (foil) behind the panelling, a low door with no lock, a heater sized for the room and a working ventilation system. Use a professional for electrical work and chimney installation.
